chunks: "An open-drain output has just one transistor, an NMOS from the pin to ground.
It can pull the line low, or it can let go, but it can never drive it high; a pull-up resistor does that. That sounds like a limitation, but it's what makes a shared bus work.
If two push-pull drivers disagree, one PMOS and one NMOS are both on, and you get a low-resistance path from supply to ground: tens of milliamps and possibly damage.
With open-drain, if two devices disagree, one pulls low and the other lets go, and low just wins. The bus acts as a wired-AND.

That wired-AND is also how I2C does its protocol tricks: multi-master arbitration, where a master that sees a 0 when it sent a 1 knows it lost; clock stretching, where a slave holds SCL low to slow the master; and the ACK, where the slave pulls SDA low during the ninth clock.
It also gives easy voltage mixing, because the high level is set by whatever rail the pull-up goes to, so two voltage domains can share the line with the right shifter.
And parts designed for it tolerate hot-plugging and being powered off on a live bus, because there's no PMOS driving high and, if the datasheet says so, no clamp from the pin to their supply.
The cost is speed and power: the rising edge is only as fast as R pC b , and the pull-up burns current whenever the line is low."
